Hatchlings of the Australian bearded dragon (Pogona barbata) emerge from their parchment-shelled eggs after an incubation period of approximately 77 days [ab = approximately 77 days] when maintained at a constant temperature of 29 °C [T = 29 °C], a duration that aligns with developmental rates observed in other agamid lizards. At the moment of eclosion, neonates exhibit a snout-vent length measuring 3.9 cm [Lb = 3.9 cm] and a wet body mass of 2.81 grams [Wwb = 2.81 grams], reflecting the limited energy reserves packaged within the egg. The initial energy content of a freshly laid egg has been calculated at 23,193.5 J  using established allometric equations, a value consistent with the relatively small clutch sizes typical of this species. This energetic investment per offspring is moderate compared to that of larger varanids, yet it provides sufficient yolk reserves to sustain the hatchling through the critical first days of exogenous feeding, during which juveniles actively forage for small arthropods among leaf litter and low vegetation. The period of yolk-sac resorption typically spans the first several days post-eclosion, during which the lecithotrophic larva relies entirely on endogenous reserves before the trophic switch to active prey capture, a transition that marks the onset of independent foraging behavior in these young reptiles.

Growth proceeds rapidly during the first year of life, with sub-adults transitioning through several distinct size classes. Puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal activation in both sexes, is attained at a snout-vent length of approximately 12.0 cm [Lp = approximately 12.0 cm], a milestone that corresponds to a wet body weight of around 56.7 grams [Wwp = around 56.7 grams] based on length-mass relationships derived from field-collected specimens. The time since birth at puberty has been estimated at 390 days [tp = 390 days] under captive conditions at a stable 25 °C [T = 25 °C], though considerable individual variation exists, with some fast-growing individuals reaching this stage as early as eight months while others require up to eighteen months. This plastic developmental trajectory is thought to be modulated by food availability and basking opportunity, both of which influence somatic growth rates and the accumulation of body condition necessary for reproductive activation.

Upon reaching reproductive maturity, adult bearded dragons exhibit a maximum snout-vent length of 25.0 cm [Li = 25.0 cm], a measurement derived from large museum series that likely represents the upper asymptotic size for the species. The corresponding ultimate wet weight in fully grown adults reaches 718.0 grams [Wwi = 718.0 grams], a substantial mass that supports the species' relatively robust, semi-arboreal habits. Females in peak condition produce up to 30 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = up to 30 eggs per clutch], and under favorable environmental conditions they can complete as many as three clutches each year [F_R_i = three clutches each year] when maintained at 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This annual reproductive output is typical of medium-sized, iteroparous agamids from temperate to subtropical habitats, where an extended breeding season allows for multiple nesting events between early spring and late summer.

The timing of first reproduction in captive populations maintained at 25 °C [T = 25 °C] occurs at a relatively advanced age compared to many small-bodied lizards. The first egg production event is typically recorded 730 days since birth [tR = 730 days since birth], a delay that reflects the substantial somatic growth required before females can allocate resources to yolk production at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This age at first reproduction is consistent with the species' moderate lifespan; maximum recorded longevity in captivity reaches 3,650 days [am = 3,650 days], or roughly ten years, though wild individuals likely experience considerably shorter lives due to predation and environmental stress at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. The combination of delayed sexual maturation and extended reproductive lifespan suggests a life-history strategy that balances high juvenile mortality with sustained annual fecundity once adulthood is achieved.

Under field conditions, bearded dragons exhibit pronounced thermoregulatory behavior that directly influences their activity budgets and metabolic expenditures. Preferred body temperatures during basking periods typically range between 32 and 36 °C, though the measurements described here were obtained under controlled laboratory conditions. The consistent thermal environment of 25 °C [T = 25 °C] used in many captive studies provides a useful baseline for comparing life-history traits across individuals, but it should be noted that natural temperature fluctuations likely modulate the precise timing of developmental events observed in the wild. Comparative data from related pogona species suggest that the relatively large body size of P. barbata, with its adult mass exceeding 700 grams, is associated with a slower pace of life than that seen in smaller agamids, including shorter daily foraging periods and a greater reliance on fat reserves during cooler months.
